I am cleaning up a messy 2K-style NCAA basketball player rating system repo and want help turning it into a respectable, easy-to-navigate portfolio repo.

I am going to upload the project files in batches of 10. Please do not make final keep/delete/archive decisions until I tell you I am done uploading everything. 

For each batch, I want you to:

* Read and identify each file
* Keep a running inventory of all uploaded files
* Briefly summarize what each file appears to do
* Flag obvious duplicates, drafts, broken files, or unclear files
* Wait for the next batch before making final repo-structure recommendations

Once I say “all files uploaded,” I want you to:

* Classify every file as Keep, Move, Archive, Delete/Exclude, or Unsure
* Recommend a clean folder structure
* Explain what each folder should contain
* Identify the main source files, final outputs, raw data, processed data, helper scripts, mapping files, reports, and junk
* Tell me what should be included in the public GitHub repo versus left out
* Help create a polished README with dashed bullet points in sections like Data Sources, Tools Used, Key Outputs, and File Guide
* Make the repo understandable to someone who did not work on the class/project

Important context:

* This was originally a class/group project, but I want to create a cleaned portfolio version
* The project is a context-aware 2K-style NCAA basketball player rating system
* It includes NCAA men’s/women’s basketball data, conference/team context, HDI-style adjustments, player rankings, possible random forest/modeling work, reports, slides, and helper scripts
* I want the final repo to look professional, not like a folder dump
* Do not assume every file belongs in the final repo
* Be direct about what is messy, redundant, or unnecessary
* If a file is important but badly named, suggest a cleaner name
* If a file should stay only for historical context, put it in archive
* If a file is required for reproducibility, say where it should go
* If the project cannot be fully reproducible, help me explain that honestly in the README

I will start uploading Batch 1 now.

Obvious Issues Already Showing
The biggest mess so far is not the idea, it is the repo hygiene:

There are multiple report versions: Context-Aware...Final Report.Rmd, GROUP06_WrittenReport.Rmd, and GROUP06_WrittenReport.pdf.

DataCheck.rmd uses hard-coded local file paths, so it is not portable.

Data file names are not self-explanatory. barttorvik_23.csv appears to contain year = 2024, and barttorvik_24.csv appears to contain year = 2025.

Mapping files are useful but informal. .txt key-value mappings are fine during a project, but a polished repo would be cleaner with team_conference_map_men.csv and team_id_conference_map.csv.

The project uses multiple data sources: HDI ratings, Bart Torvik/cbbdata, ESPN/wehoop, schedules, and manual mapping. That is good portfolio-wise, but it means the README will need a very clear reproducibility note.

The slide deck and written report both clearly explain the project’s core framing: box-score production, team strength, schedule difficulty, and conference strength. Those are likely strong public-facing artifacts.

  }

    grid-template-columns: 1fr;

View project

Additional Analytics Work
Beyond my main basketball projects, I’ve worked on applied analytics projects involving Monte Carlo simulation, survey analysis, employee attrition modeling, and statistical reporting. These projects use the same core process: cleaning messy data, building reproducible workflows, modeling uncertainty, and communicating results clearly.

About
My background sits between statistics, sports media, and communication, which has shaped how I think about analytics. I care about the model or method, but I also care about whether the result can be understood, trusted, and used.

A lot of strong analysis gets ignored because it is trapped in a spreadsheet, buried in a notebook, or presented in a way that does not match the audience. I’m interested in closing that gap by turning messy data into something clear, visual, and worth engaging with.

Most of my work is built in R using Quarto, Shiny, R Markdown, ggplot2, tidyverse, and API-based data workflows.
:::

Context-Aware NCAA Basketball Player Ratings
Tools: R, randomForest, tidyverse, Bart Torvik data, ESPN/wehoop, hoopR, cbbdata, R Markdown

Built a context-aware player rating system for NCAA men’s and women’s basketball that converts box-score production, team strength, schedule difficulty, and conference context into 2K-style 40–99 ratings. The project was originally developed as a class/group project and later cleaned into a structured portfolio repo with organized scripts, final outputs, reports, and documentation.

The men’s pipeline used Bart Torvik player statistics joined with HDI ratings as a modeling baseline. The women’s pipeline used ESPN box-score data through wehoop, with season-level aggregation, team/conference mapping, and rating adjustments built to make the outputs more comparable across competitive environments.



Pipeline diagram showing how men’s and women’s player data were cleaned, modeled, adjusted for team and conference context, and converted into final 2K-style ratings.

Highlights

Trained a random forest model to estimate player ratings from box-score and efficiency statistics

Built men’s and women’s pipelines using different data sources and normalization steps

Applied team strength, schedule difficulty, and conference strength adjustments

Produced final men’s and women’s 40–99 player rating tables

Cleaned a messy class project into a professional GitHub repo with clear folders, scripts, outputs, and documentation

View project repository

title: "Caleb Ramsey"

::: {.hero}
<div class="tagline">Analytics · data visualization · applied sports technology</div>

# Caleb Ramsey

<div class="subtitle">
Virginia Tech Statistics and Sports Media & Analytics graduate building data tools, visual reports, and reproducible workflows in R. My work sits at the intersection of basketball, analytics, and communication, including team-facing dashboards, scouting systems, public NBA/WNBA analysis, and prototype player evaluation models.
</div>
:::

## Featured Work

::: {.project-grid}

::: {.project-card}
![](assets/images/practice-dashboard-example.png)

### Practice Hustle Dashboard

Built a locally hosted Quarto dashboard for Virginia Tech Women’s Basketball to turn daily practice tracking data into coach-facing summaries, leaderboards, player pages, and team trends.

[View project](projects.qmd#practice-hustle-dashboard)
:::

::: {.project-card}
![](assets/images/liz-kitley-scout-card-example.png)

### Scouting Card & Badge System

Designed custom basketball badges in Photoshop and built an R pipeline that converts Synergy playtype data into automated player scouting cards.

[View project](projects.qmd#scouting-card--badge-system)
:::

::: {.project-card}
![](assets/images/ncaa-2k-ratings-pipeline.png)

## Additional Analytics Work

Beyond my main basketball projects, I’ve worked on applied analytics projects involving Monte Carlo simulation, survey analysis, employee attrition modeling, and statistical reporting. These projects use the same core process: cleaning messy data, building reproducible workflows, modeling uncertainty, and communicating results clearly.

## About

My background combines statistics, sports media, and communication, which has shaped how I think about analytics. I care about the model or method, but I also care about whether the result can be understood, trusted, and used by people who do not live in the data every day.

A lot of strong analysis gets ignored because it is trapped in a spreadsheet, buried in a notebook, or presented in a way that does not match the audience. I’m interested in closing that gap by turning messy data into something clear, visual, and worth engaging with.


Most of my work is built in R using Quarto, Shiny, R Markdown, ggplot2, tidyverse, and API-based data workflows.
